summary: Defines the Extensible Authentication Protocol, a framework that supports many authentication methods. It usually runs directly over link layers such as PPP or IEEE 802, without IP, and handles its own retransmission. It obsoletes RFC 2284 and was updated by RFC 5247 and RFC 7057.

eli5.summary: Before you may join a network, you must prove who you are. EAP is a flexible envelope that can carry many different ways of proving it.

subtitle: A flexible envelope that lets a network ask a device to prove who it is, using almost any authentication method.

tldr.problem: Networks need to authenticate devices before granting access, often on links where IP is not available yet, and they do not want to rebuild every switch or access point each time a new authentication method appears.
tldr.mechanism: EAP is a lock-step Request and Response exchange. The authenticator asks, the peer answers, and the conversation ends with a Success or Failure packet. The actual authentication logic lives in separate methods, which may run on a backend server while the authenticator just passes packets through.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3748 obsoletes RFC 2284 and was updated by RFC 5247 and RFC 7057. EAP leaves security to its methods, so each method must state its own security claims.

today: RFC 3748 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2284 and has been updated by RFC 5247 and RFC 7057. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What EAP Is For
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is an authentication framework that supports multiple authentication methods. It typically runs directly over data link layers such as the Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) or IEEE 802, without requiring IP. It provides its own duplicate elimination and retransmission, but it relies on the lower layer to deliver packets in order. EAP itself does not fragment packets, although individual methods may.

EAP selects a specific authentication mechanism, typically after the authenticator asks for more information. Instead of updating the authenticator for every new method, a backend authentication server can implement the methods while the authenticator acts as a pass-through.

The RFC limits the scope on purpose. EAP was designed for network access authentication, where IP connectivity may not be available. Using it for other purposes such as bulk data transport is NOT RECOMMENDED, because it is a lock-step protocol with a single packet in flight.
sections.eli5: EAP is like a doorman who does not check IDs himself. He passes a note to a helper who knows how to check many kinds of ID, and then lets you in or turns you away.

sections.title: The Request and Response Conversation
sections.content:
Three roles appear throughout. The authenticator is the end of the link that starts authentication. The peer is the end that responds (IEEE 802.1X calls it the Supplicant). The EAP server is the entity that ends the authentication method with the peer, which is either the authenticator itself or a backend server.

The exchange runs in steps. The authenticator sends a Request with a Type field, such as Identity or MD5-Challenge. The peer sends a Response of the matching Type. Requests and Responses continue as long as needed. EAP is lock-step: apart from the first Request, a new Request cannot be sent before a valid Response arrives. The conversation ends when the authenticator sends a Success (Code 3) or a Failure (Code 4). The authenticator MUST NOT send Success or Failure when it is merely retransmitting or when it gets no response.

An initial Identity Request is typical but not required. The identity may already be known from the port, the calling station identity or the MAC address.

A conversation MAY use a sequence of methods, but only one authentication method (Type 4 or greater) may be used, after which the authenticator MUST send Success or Failure. Multiple methods are not supported because of their vulnerability to man-in-the-middle attacks. A tunneled method, which runs other methods inside one, appears to EAP as a single method and is exempt, but it MUST protect against man-in-the-middle attacks.
sections.eli5: It is a game of question and answer where the doorman asks one question at a time and waits for your answer before asking the next. At the end he says either "come in" or "no entry".

sections.title: Layers, Pass-Through and Peer-to-Peer
sections.content:
The RFC describes an EAP implementation as four layers: the lower layer that carries EAP frames, the EAP layer that handles duplicate detection and retransmission, the EAP peer and authenticator layers, and the EAP method layers. An implementation does not have to follow this model as long as the on-the-wire behavior is consistent with it.

The Code field works much like a protocol number in IP: Requests, Successes and Failures go to the peer layer, and Responses go to the authenticator layer. The Type field works much like a port number in UDP or TCP, steering a packet to the right method.

In pass-through mode, the authenticator forwards Responses to the backend server and forwards Requests, Successes and Failures back to the peer, normally deciding only from the Code, Identifier and Length fields. A compliant pass-through authenticator MUST by default forward packets of any Type, and it MUST decide the outcome only from the Accept or Reject indication from the backend server. RADIUS and Diameter support only pass-through authenticator operation, not pass-through peers.

EAP is also peer-to-peer: both ends may authenticate each other at the same time, and the text lists reasons why two authentications, one in each direction, can still be needed.
sections.eli5: The doorman can check a few IDs himself, but for most visitors he just walks the paperwork to the office in the back and does whatever the office says.

sections.title: What EAP Expects From the Link Below
sections.content:
EAP makes several assumptions about its lower layer. It does not assume the lower layer is reliable, because the authenticator retransmits unanswered Requests. It does rely on lower layer error detection, since methods may not protect every header field. It can function when the lower layer provides an EAP MTU of 1020 octets or greater, and methods can assume that minimum. Methods that may exceed it SHOULD support fragmentation and reassembly themselves.

EAP does not require the Identifier to increase, so it depends on the lower layer to preserve ordering. Reordering will typically cause an authentication failure. Running EAP over raw IP or UDP is NOT RECOMMENDED, while encapsulation within RADIUS satisfies the ordering requirement.

Within PPP, exactly one EAP packet is carried in a frame whose protocol field is hex C227, and EAP is negotiated through the Authentication Protocol Configuration Option. This lets the specific mechanism be chosen later, in the Authentication Phase. Within IEEE 802, the encapsulation comes from IEEE 802.1X and involves no PPP, so non-EAP mechanisms such as PAP or CHAP cannot be negotiated.

Retransmission is the authenticator's job. Where the lower layer is unreliable, the timer SHOULD be estimated dynamically and a maximum of 3-5 retransmissions is suggested. Over a reliable lower layer, the timer SHOULD be set to an infinite value so no retransmission happens at the EAP layer.
sections.eli5: The doorman's notes must arrive in the order they were written and not be smudged on the way. EAP trusts the road for that, but it will repeat a question if no answer comes back.

sections.title: The EAP Packet
sections.content:
Every EAP packet starts with three fields: Code (one octet), Identifier (one octet) and Length (two octets, covering the whole EAP packet), followed by Data. The Codes are 1 Request, 2 Response, 3 Success and 4 Failure. Packets with any other Code MUST be silently discarded. Octets beyond the Length are treated as link layer padding and ignored, while a packet whose Length is larger than the octets received MUST be silently discarded.

Request and Response packets add a one-octet Type and variable Type-Data. The Identifier matches a Response to its Request. Retransmitted Requests MUST keep the same Identifier, while any new Request MUST change it. A Response whose Identifier does not match the outstanding Request MUST be silently discarded. If a peer receives a valid duplicate Request, it MUST resend its original Response without reprocessing it.

Success and Failure packets are only four octets long, carry no Type and MUST NOT contain additional data. Because they are not acknowledged, they are not retransmitted and may be lost. A peer MUST silently discard a "canned" Success sent immediately on connection, so a rogue authenticator cannot skip mutual authentication.
sections.eli5: Every EAP note has a little header saying what kind of note it is, which question it belongs to and how long it is. The final "yes" or "no" note is only the header.

sections.title: Method Types and Negotiation
sections.content:
The Type field says what a Request or Response is about. The first three are special: Identity (1) asks who the peer is, Notification (2) conveys a displayable message from the authenticator, and Nak (3) is valid only in a Response. The RFC also defines MD5-Challenge (4), One Time Password (5) and Generic Token Card (6). All implementations MUST support Types 1-4 and SHOULD support Type 254.

The Identity Response is recommended mainly for routing and for choosing a method, because Identity exchanges are sent in cleartext. MD5-Challenge is analogous to PPP CHAP. The RFC does not define a cleartext password method on purpose, and the OTP and GTC methods MUST NOT be used to carry cleartext passwords (GTC only with a protected tunnel with server authentication).

Methods are negotiated with the Nak. If the peer cannot accept the Requested Type, it replies with a Nak listing the Types it would accept, one octet per Type, or a zero to say it has no alternative. A peer MUST NOT send a Nak after it has already sent a non-Nak Response. An Expanded Nak does the same job for Expanded Types.

Expanded Types (254) add a 3-octet Vendor-Id and a 4-octet Vendor-Type. A Vendor-Id of 0 is reserved for the IETF and extends the global method Type space. Type 255 is Experimental. For IANA, new Packet Codes need Standards Action, and method Types 46-191 and 20 may be allocated on the advice of a Designated Expert with Specification Required.
sections.eli5: If the doorman asks for one kind of ID and you do not have it, you can answer "I have these other kinds instead". Some visitors even carry special ID cards from one company only.

sections.title: Threats and Security Claims
sections.content:
EAP assumes an attacker may reach the link. The threat list includes snooping identities, modifying or spoofing packets, denial of service through spoofed Success or Failure packets, offline dictionary attacks, man-in-the-middle attacks, forcing a weak method, weak key derivation, weak ciphersuites, and a dishonest authenticator providing incorrect information.

Because the EAP layer gives no per-packet protection, the RFC requires every EAP method specification to include a Security Claims section. It states the mechanism, the claimed properties (mutual authentication, integrity protection, replay protection, confidentiality, key derivation, dictionary attack resistance, fast reconnect, cryptographic binding), the key strength, the key hierarchy and which claims are NOT made. Each method defined in the RFC lists its own claims; for example, MD5-Challenge claims no mutual authentication and no dictionary attack protection.

Several specific risks are covered. Tunneling EAP can allow a man-in-the-middle when the tunnel does not authenticate the peer, and cryptographic binding is one mitigation. Nak packets are unprotected, so a peer should have exactly one method per named identity to avoid negotiation attacks. With one-way methods such as EAP-MD5, the peer does not authenticate the authenticator. A compromised pass-through authenticator can give misleading information to the peer, which channel binding is meant to detect.
sections.eli5: Bad guys might listen in, send fake notes or trick the doorman into using the weakest check. So every kind of ID check has to publish a list of what it protects against and what it does not.

sections.title: Key Derivation
sections.content:
A method that supports key derivation MUST export a Master Session Key (MSK) of at least 64 octets and an Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) of at least 64 octets, and it MUST provide mutual authentication between peer and server. The MSK and EMSK MUST NOT be used directly to protect data. They are large enough to derive an AAA-Key, which is then used to derive Transient Session Keys for the chosen ciphersuite.

The EMSK is reserved for future use. It MUST remain on the EAP peer and EAP server and MUST NOT be transported to other parties. Methods SHOULD ensure freshness, and a RECOMMENDED way is for each party to contribute a nonce of at least 128 bits. Methods SHOULD be capable of an effective key strength of at least 128 bits, and SHOULD reuse well established key derivation mechanisms such as those in IKE or TLS rather than inventing new ones.

When the authenticator and the authentication server are separate machines, authentication happens between the peer and the server, not the authenticator. The AAA protocol between them MUST support per-packet authentication, integrity and replay protection, because the authenticator learns the outcome only from the AAA protocol.
sections.eli5: When the ID check is done, the two sides can also agree on a secret code. They never use that master code directly. They use it to make fresh secret codes for the actual conversation afterwards.
